A2.text:
Nigar and her brother Murad live together in a small flat near Nizami Street. They are very different people. Nigar is always neat and quiet, but Murad is loud and messy. However, the siblings have a very strong bond. They share all the household chores every week. Nigar cooks tasty meals, and Murad cleans the floors and washes dishes.

This Sunday, a special relative is coming to visit. Their Aunt Aysel is arriving from Sheki. She is the oldest person in their family tree.

“We must make a great dinner,” Nigar said. “Aunt Aysel likes perfect houses. We cannot disappoint her today.”

They worked hard all morning. Nigar cooked a big pot of plov. Murad cleaned the windows and the kitchen. He even bought fresh baklava from the bakery.

At six o'clock, Aunt Aysel arrived. She looked around the clean flat and smiled. Then, she walked into the kitchen. Murad was eating a piece of baklava before dinner. He had sugar on his shirt and his hands.

Aunt Aysel laughed loudly. “Murad, you are just like your father!” she said. “The apple doesn't fall far from the tree.”

Nigar smiled and hugged her aunt. It was a wonderful evening. They were family — flesh and blood — and nothing was better than living under one roof together.

questions.q: Why are Nigar and Murad cleaning and cooking so much on Sunday?
options: They are preparing for their Aunt Aysel's visit
They want to sell their flat
It is Murad's birthday party
They always do this every Sunday
questions.why: “This Sunday, a special relative is coming to visit. Their Aunt Aysel is arriving from Sheki.”

questions.q: What does Murad do to help in the flat?
options: He cooks the plov
He paints the windows
He cleans the floors and washes dishes
He fixes the television
questions.why: “Nigar cooks tasty meals, and Murad cleans the floors and washes dishes.”

questions.q: What did Murad have on his shirt when his aunt saw him?
options: Sugar
Tomato sauce
Water
Dirt from the windows
questions.why: “He had sugar on his shirt and his hands.”

questions.q: Aunt Aysel was very angry because Murad was eating before dinner.
options: True
False
Not given
questions.why: “Aunt Aysel laughed loudly.”

questions.q: The siblings share all the “household chores”. What are chores?
options: Delicious family meals
Regular tasks you do at home like cleaning
Rooms in a small flat
Arguments between brothers and sisters
questions.why: The text says they share household chores: “Nigar cooks tasty meals, and Murad cleans the floors and washes dishes.”

questions.q: Why does Aunt Aysel say Murad is like his father?
options: Because his father also liked to eat sweets and make a mess
Because he is wearing his father's shirt
Because his father also cleaned the windows
Because his father lives in Sheki
questions.why: She sees Murad eating baklava with sugar on his shirt and laughs, saying “Murad, you are just like your father!”

B1.text:
Nigar and her younger brother Murad share a flat near Nizami Street. Although they grew up with the same traditional upbringing, the two siblings are complete opposites. Nigar is incredibly organized, while Murad leaves a trail of chaos wherever he goes. Despite this, they share a very close bond and manage to live peacefully under one roof by dividing the household chores fairly.

This weekend, they were preparing for a special guest. Their great-aunt Aysel was travelling all the way from Sheki. As the oldest living relative on their family tree, her visits were a major event.

“Aunt Aysel notices everything,” Nigar warned, wiping the kitchen counter for the third time. “We need to show her that we can look after ourselves properly.”

They spent Saturday cleaning the flat from top to bottom. Nigar prepared a traditional plov, and Murad went out to buy the best baklava he could find. However, Murad had a weakness for sweets. When he was a boy, his grandmother used to spoil him with sugary treats, and he had never grown out of the habit.

When Aunt Aysel finally arrived, she took off her coat and smiled at the spotless living room. Then, she walked into the kitchen to greet her nephew. Murad was standing by the fridge, quickly finishing a piece of baklava. Powdered sugar was sprinkled all over his dark shirt.

Instead of criticizing him, Aunt Aysel burst into laughter. “Oh, Murad! You are exactly like your father was at your age,” she said warmly. “The apple doesn't fall far from the tree, does it?”

Nigar relaxed and poured the tea. Looking at her messy brother and her laughing aunt, she realized that family wasn't about having a perfect home. They were flesh and blood, and that was what truly mattered.

questions.q: What happens when the siblings try to present a perfect home for their aunt?
options: The aunt is disappointed and decides to leave early
Their aunt arrives and finds Murad making a mess, but she finds it funny and sweet
They have a big argument and burn the dinner
Murad forgets to buy the dessert and ruins the meal
questions.why: Aunt Aysel catches Murad eating baklava with sugar on his shirt, but instead of criticizing him, she bursts into laughter.

questions.q: How do Nigar and Murad manage to live together peacefully?
options: They never see each other during the week
Nigar does all the cleaning by herself
They order food instead of cooking
By dividing the household chores fairly
questions.why: “...manage to live peacefully under one roof by dividing the household chores fairly.”

questions.q: Why did Murad eat the baklava before dinner?
options: He had not eaten anything all day
Nigar told him to taste it first
He wanted to hide it from his aunt
He had a weakness for sweets because his grandmother used to spoil him
questions.why: “Murad had a weakness for sweets. When he was a boy, his grandmother used to spoil him with sugary treats...”

questions.q: Nigar was angry with Aunt Aysel for laughing at Murad.
options: True
False
Not given
questions.why: “Nigar relaxed and poured the tea. Looking at her messy brother and her laughing aunt, she realized that family wasn't about having a perfect home.”

questions.q: The text says their grandmother used to “spoil” Murad. What does this mean?
options: To teach a child how to cook
To punish a child for bad behavior
To make someone clean the house
To give a child too much of what they want
questions.why: She gave him too many sugary treats, creating a habit he never grew out of.

questions.q: What does Nigar learn at the end of the story?
options: That she should not ask Murad to buy sweets
That a strong family connection is more important than a tidy house
That she needs to clean the kitchen again
That Aunt Aysel prefers plov over baklava
questions.why: “she realized that family wasn't about having a perfect home. They were flesh and blood, and that was what truly mattered.”

B2.text:
Nigar and her younger brother Murad shared a surprisingly peaceful flat just a stone’s throw from Nizami Street. Despite sharing the same strict upbringing, the siblings possessed completely opposite temperaments. Nigar was methodical and deeply organized, whereas Murad seemed to generate a mild tornado of chaos wherever he walked. Yet, their bond was unbreakable. They managed to survive under one roof without daily arguments simply by splitting the household chores down the middle.

This particular weekend, the stakes were high. Their formidable great-aunt Aysel was travelling down from Sheki. As the most senior living relative on their expanding family tree, her rare visits felt more like official inspections than casual family gatherings.

“Aunt Aysel has an eagle eye for dust,” Nigar muttered, aggressively polishing the kitchen counters. “We need to prove that we’re responsible adults who can maintain a respectable home.”

They spent the entirety of Saturday scrubbing the apartment. Nigar slow-cooked a magnificent saffron plov, while Murad was sent on a mission to Yasil Bazar to procure the finest baklava in the city. Unfortunately, Murad had a lifelong weakness for pastries. As a young boy, their late grandmother used to spoil him rotten with extra desserts, a habit he had fully carried into his twenties.

When Aunt Aysel finally swept into the flat that evening, she removed her silk scarf and nodded approvingly at the gleaming living room. Satisfied, she marched toward the kitchen to greet her nephew.

She stopped in the doorway. Murad was leaning against the refrigerator, hurriedly chewing a large slice of baklava before dinner. A generous dusting of powdered sugar covered the front of his dark sweater, and he froze like a deer in the headlights.

For a second, the room was completely silent. Then, instead of lecturing him, Aunt Aysel let out a booming laugh. “Oh, Murad! You are the spitting image of your father,” she chuckled. “The apple doesn't fall far from the tree, does it? He was always stealing sweets before dinner too.”

Nigar let out a long sigh of relief and poured the tea. Looking at them, she realized that maintaining a flawless house was secondary. They were flesh and blood, and those imperfect, shared quirks were exactly what made them a family.

words.phrase: has an eagle eye for dust
froze like a deer in the headlights
let out a long sigh of relief

questions.q: What is the central theme of the story?
options: That siblings can never truly live together in peace
That traditional Azerbaijani meals take a long time to prepare
That elderly relatives are always impossible to please
That family bonds and shared traits matter more than keeping a flawless home
questions.why: Nigar realizes at the end that despite the mess, their shared quirks and “flesh and blood” connection are what make them a family.

questions.q: How does the author describe Nigar and Murad's personalities?
options: They are both extremely neat and methodical
They both generate a tornado of chaos
They have completely opposite temperaments
They are shy and avoid visitors
questions.why: “...the siblings possessed completely opposite temperaments. Nigar was methodical... whereas Murad seemed to generate a mild tornado of chaos...”

questions.q: Why did Nigar feel pressured to polish the kitchen counters?
options: Because they were going to sell the apartment
Because Murad had spilled tea on them
Because Aunt Aysel treats her visits like official inspections
Because she was bored on a Saturday
questions.why: “As the most senior living relative... her rare visits felt more like official inspections... ‘Aunt Aysel has an eagle eye for dust,’ Nigar muttered”

questions.q: Murad baked the baklava himself in the flat.
options: True
False
Not given
questions.why: “Murad was sent on a mission to Yasil Bazar to procure the finest baklava in the city.”

questions.q: Nigar and Murad had the same strict “upbringing”. What does “upbringing” mean?
options: The way a child is raised and taught by their family
The school they attended in Baku
The genetic traits they inherited
The neighborhood where they currently live
questions.why: Upbringing refers to how children are raised, which explains why they share this background despite different temperaments.

questions.q: How did Murad likely feel when Aunt Aysel stopped in the doorway?
options: He was proud of the dessert he bought
He was angry that she interrupted his snack
He was panicked and thought he was going to be scolded
He was excited to show her his clean sweater
questions.why: “he froze like a deer in the headlights.” This idiom implies he was caught by surprise and very frightened or panicked.

podcast.title: Seven under one roof

hosts.Leyla: lives in Baku and loves a good plan
hosts.Sam: grew up in Manchester and once travelled with no plan at all

before.predict: How many people lived in your home when you were a child? Guess: how many lived in Leyla's?

lines.t: Hi everyone, and welcome to the SpeakLab Podcast. I'm Leyla.
And I'm Sam. Today's topic is family and home. Leyla, how many people lived in your house when you were a child?
[laugh] Seven! My grandparents, my parents, my brother, my sister and me — all under one roof.
Seven people and one bathroom?
Two, thank goodness. But the mornings were still a battle. How about you?
I have two older sisters. When we were kids, we argued about everything — the TV, the front seat of the car, the last biscuit.
That's normal with siblings. My brother and I fought all the time, but now he's my best friend. The bond is really strong.
Same with my sisters. We have a group chat, and we talk every day.
Did you have to do chores at home?
Oh yes. I washed the dishes every evening, and on Saturdays I cleaned the car. My mum paid me one pound a week.
One pound! We didn't get money. My grandmother said helping at home is just what family does.
Was she strict?
With my parents, very. With us grandchildren? Not at all. She spoiled us completely — sweets, money, staying up late.
[chuckle] Grandparents are the same everywhere. My mum spoils my sisters' kids now.
My niece Aysu is making a family tree for school. She called me yesterday with a hundred questions.
That's a great project. How far back can she go?
To my great-grandparents. After that, nobody remembers. Some relatives moved away long ago, and we lost contact.
My dad tried to make our family tree too. And he tells terrible jokes — exactly like me.
[laugh] Well, the apple doesn't fall far from the tree.
Ha! A family tree joke. I'm proud of you.
Here's your question for your next SpeakLab call: who is the person in your family you are most like — and how?
For me, it's my dad. Sadly. See you next time!
Bye for now!

questions.q: What is the episode mainly about?
options: Big families, brothers and sisters, chores and family memories
How to cook for seven people
A trip abroad
School projects about trees
questions.why: They compare growing up in a big family in Baku and in England.

questions.q: How many people lived in Leyla's home when she was a child?
options: Four
Five
Seven
Nine
questions.why: "Seven! … all under one roof."

questions.q: What chores did Sam do?
options: He cooked dinner
He washed the dishes and cleaned the car
He walked the dog
He did the shopping
questions.why: "I washed the dishes every evening, and on Saturdays I cleaned the car."

questions.q: Leyla's grandmother was strict with her grandchildren.
options: True
False
Not given
questions.why: "With us grandchildren? Not at all."

questions.q: "The apple doesn't fall far from the tree" means…
options: Children are often like their parents
Apples are good for you
Families live close together
Trees are important
questions.why: Sam tells bad jokes, just like his dad.

questions.q: Why can't Aysu go further back than her great-grandparents?
options: She is too young
Nobody remembers, and the family lost contact with some relatives
Her teacher told her to stop
There are no photos
questions.why: "After that, nobody remembers… we lost contact."

words: The apple doesn't fall far from the tree
talk: Who is the person in your family you are most like — and how?
Did you do chores when you were a child? Which one did you hate?
